brier.what: The mean squared error of a probability forecast against what actually happened (outcome coded 0 or 1). Lower is better; 0 is perfect, 0.25 is what a permanent coin-flip forecast of 50% scores.
brier.coined: Glenn W. Brier, 1950, in "Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability" (Monthly Weather Review) — invented so weather forecasters saying "70% chance of rain" could be graded honestly.
brier.intuition: If you say 90% and it happens, you're barely punished (0.1 squared = 0.01). Say 90% and it doesn't happen, you lose big (0.9 squared = 0.81). So the only way to score well long-run is to say what you really believe — bluffing confidence costs you.
brier.math: BS = mean of (p − y)² over all forecasts, where p is the stated probability (0..1) and y is the outcome (1 if it happened, 0 if not). It is a strictly proper scoring rule: your expected score is best when you report your true belief.
brier.here: Every settled tier-2 window gets a Brier for each kb arm and one for the Kalshi market itself (btc_rl/online.py; per-arm tables in scripts/run_audit.py tier2 section). Shown on metrics_lab.html, sev0.html, live_online.html, ab_dashboard.html.
brier.code:
r["brier"] = round((r["p_up"] - outcome) ** 2, 4)   # btc_rl/online.py
r["mkt_brier"] = round((r["mkt_p_up"] - outcome) ** 2, 4)
brier.src: Murphy decomposition of the Brier score: https://rmets.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/qj.2985 (see docs/RESEARCH_BASELINE.md 2.1)

brier-skill.what: One number answering "does this forecaster beat a reference forecaster?" — computed from the two Brier scores. Positive means better than the reference; 1 is perfect; negative means worse.
brier-skill.coined: The skill-score convention comes from mid-20th-century meteorological forecast verification (the Murphy lineage of Brier decomposition); exact first use of "Brier skill score" not verified here.
brier-skill.intuition: A weather forecaster in a desert who says "no rain" every day looks amazing until you compare against the trivial forecast that says the same thing. Skill = how much of the remaining error you removed relative to the reference.
brier-skill.math: BSS = 1 − BS_forecaster / BS_reference. Our references: the market's own Brier (bss_mkt) and 0.25, the coin-flip climatology (bss_clim). BSS of 0.1 means 10% less squared error than the reference.
brier-skill.here: btc_rl/metrics.py brier_skill(); btc_rl/online.py reports bss_mkt and bss_clim per kb arm — "does any arm beat the Kalshi market" is exactly this number. Surfaced on metrics_lab.html (kb arms table) and experiment_review.html.
brier-skill.code:
def brier_skill(brier, reference):        # btc_rl/metrics.py
    return 1 - brier / reference          # >0 beats the reference

mse.what: The average of squared prediction errors. Squaring makes big misses count much more than small ones and makes the math smooth to optimize.
mse.coined: Squared-error loss descends from least squares — Legendre published it in 1805, Gauss claimed use from 1795. The acronym "MSE" is standard 20th-century statistics; exact attribution of the name not verified here.
mse.intuition: Being $10 off once hurts more than being $1 off ten times (100 vs 10 after squaring). That is a choice: MSE says rare big errors are what you care about most.
mse.math: MSE = mean of (predicted − actual)². Its minimizer is the conditional mean — predicting the average outcome is the optimal MSE strategy.
mse.here: The headline tier-1 price error (the project switched its headline from MAE to MSE on 2026-08-28, NOTES metric-switch entry). Computed in btc_rl/online.py and scripts/run_audit.py tier1; shown on metrics_lab.html, live_training.html, experiment_review.html.
mse.code: mse = sum(e*e for e in errs) / len(errs)   # errs = pred - actual, dollars
mse.src: docs/RESEARCH_BASELINE.md 1.1/gap 7 (why raw MSE alone is not comparable across regimes)

mae.what: The average of absolute prediction errors, in the same units as the thing predicted (dollars here). Robust: a $100 miss counts exactly 100, not 10,000.
mae.coined: Absolute-error loss traces to Laplace's 18th-century work on estimation; the "MAE" name is standard modern statistics — exact attribution not verified here.
mae.intuition: "On average, how many dollars off were we?" — the most literal possible error question. Its optimal strategy is predicting the median outcome, not the mean.
mae.math: MAE = mean of |predicted − actual|. Minimized by the conditional median, so it is less swayed by fat-tailed jumps than MSE.
mae.here: Kept alongside MSE for every tier-1 arm (abs_err per row in btc_rl/online.py); MASE is built on it. Visible in metrics_lab.html and index.html tables.
mae.code: abs_err = abs(pred_price - actual_price)   # per settled prediction row

rmse.what: The square root of MSE — same ranking of models as MSE, but back in the original units (dollars), so it is readable.
rmse.coined: Same least-squares lineage as MSE (Legendre 1805 / Gauss); the acronym's coinage not verified here.
rmse.intuition: MSE of 2500 dollars-squared means nothing to a human; RMSE of $50 does. It is a "typical miss size" that leans toward the bigger misses.
rmse.math: RMSE = sqrt(mean((pred − actual)²)). Always ≥ MAE; the gap between them measures how much the errors vary in size.
rmse.here: btc_rl/metrics.py rmse(); reported per tier-1 arm in btc_rl/online.py and btc_rl/train.py; on metrics_lab.html and experiment_review.html.
rmse.code:
def rmse(errs):                            # btc_rl/metrics.py
    return math.sqrt(sum(e*e for e in errs) / len(errs))

mase.what: Your MAE divided by the MAE of the naive "no-change" forecast on the same slots. Below 1 = you beat doing nothing; above 1 = the do-nothing forecast beat you.
mase.coined: Proposed by Rob Hyndman & Anne Koehler, 2006 ("Another look at measures of forecast accuracy", International Journal of Forecasting) as the standard scale-free accuracy measure, because percentage errors degenerate in common situations.
mase.intuition: Saying "my error was $12" is meaningless without knowing how hard the series is. MASE grades you against the laziest possible forecaster — "price in 15 minutes = price now". In efficient markets that lazy forecaster is shockingly hard to beat.
mase.math: MASE = mean(|your errors|) / mean(|naive errors|), both measured on the same time slots. The naive forecast here is persistence (last observed price).
mase.here: btc_rl/metrics.py mase(); computed per arm x horizon in btc_rl/online.py (naive errors from the same made_ts slots). Shown on metrics_lab.html, index.html, experiment_review.html. Research gap #7: make it the tier-1 headline.

msse.what: The squared-loss twin of MASE: your MSE divided by the naive forecast's MSE on the same slots. Below 1 beats the naive floor.
msse.coined: Part of the scaled-error family that followed Hyndman & Koehler's 2006 MASE; the specific MSSE name appears in later forecasting texts — exact attribution not verified here.
msse.intuition: Same referee as MASE, but with MSE's rulebook: big misses hurt quadratically. Kept alongside MASE because squared loss is outlier-sensitive in fat-tailed series like BTC.
msse.math: MSSE = mean(e²) / mean(e_naive²), both on identical slots. Added when this project's headline switched MAE → MSE so the scaled view matched the headline loss.
msse.here: btc_rl/metrics.py msse() (added 2026-08-28); computed next to MASE in btc_rl/online.py; on experiment_review.html.
msse.code:
naive = sum(e*e for e in naive_abs_errs) / len(naive_abs_errs)
return (sum(e*e for e in abs_errs) / len(abs_errs)) / naive   # btc_rl/metrics.py

pinball.what: The standard score for interval/quantile forecasts. It rewards bands that are narrow AND still contain the truth — coverage alone can be gamed by making bands huge.
pinball.coined: The underlying check function is Koenker & Bassett's quantile regression loss (1978, Econometrica). The "pinball" nickname (the loss graph looks like a ball bouncing off a flipper) — origin: forecasting community, exact attribution not verified here.
pinball.intuition: If you promise "the price will be between A and B 80% of the time", a giant band always wins on coverage but tells nobody anything. Pinball charges rent for width: every dollar of band costs you, misses cost you more.
pinball.math: For quantile q and prediction z: loss = q·(y − z) if y ≥ z, else (1−q)·(z − y). We average the loss of the 10% edge (lo) and the 90% edge (hi) of the 80% band.
pinball.here: btc_rl/metrics.py pinball(); scored per tier-1 band in scripts/run_audit.py (research gap #2 closed: coverage-only band scoring was the defect). On metrics_lab.html and experiment_review.html.
pinball.src: M5 Uncertainty used scaled pinball loss: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0169207021001722 (docs/RESEARCH_BASELINE.md 1.3)

auc.what: Area Under the ROC Curve: the probability that a randomly chosen winner gets a higher score than a randomly chosen loser. 0.5 = no ranking skill (coin flip), 1.0 = perfect ranking.
auc.coined: ROC (receiver operating characteristic) analysis came from WWII radar signal-detection work and 1950s psychophysics (Green & Swets); AUC was popularized for evaluation by Hanley & McNeil, 1982 (Radiology).
auc.intuition: Ignore whether the stated numbers are honest — just ask: when the model likes A more than B, is A actually more likely to happen? AUC measures pure ordering skill, separate from calibration.
auc.math: AUC = P(score(random positive) > score(random negative)), computable as the Mann-Whitney U statistic normalized by n_pos x n_neg, with ties counted half.
auc.here: Computed in-page from the settled kb rows (Mann-Whitney with tie handling — site/metrics_lab.html and site/sev0.html share the same JS implementation). "AUC — ranking skill" section of metrics_lab.html; mixed-arm confidence AUC on sev0.html.
auc.code:
/* site/metrics_lab.html — Mann-Whitney AUC with tie handling */
auc = (rankSumPos - nPos*(nPos+1)/2) / (nPos * nNeg)

log-loss.what: The negative log of the probability you assigned to what actually happened. Confidently wrong is catastrophic: saying 99% and being wrong costs log(100) ≈ 4.6, versus 0.69 for an honest 50%.
log-loss.coined: The logarithmic scoring rule was proposed by I. J. Good (1952, "Rational Decisions"); its information-theoretic root is Shannon's 1948 entropy.
log-loss.intuition: Imagine paying rent equal to your surprise. If you said an event was near-impossible and it happened, you are infinitely surprised — log loss actually charges you for that. It punishes overconfidence harder than Brier does.
log-loss.math: LL = −[y·log(p) + (1−y)·log(1−p)], averaged over forecasts. Like Brier, strictly proper: honesty is the optimal policy.
log-loss.here: The calibrator's scoreboard: PlattCalibrator keeps a decayed prequential log-loss for calibrated vs raw probabilities (btc_rl/agents.py — "did calibrating beat not calibrating?"), and FixedShare weights arms by per-window log-loss (btc_rl/treatments.py). Shown on metrics_lab.html kb table and sev0.html.
log-loss.code:
ll = -(y*math.log(p) + (1-y)*math.log(1-p))
self.ll = decay*self.ll + ll                # decayed scoreboard, agents.py

calibration.what: A forecaster is calibrated when its stated probabilities match reality's frequencies: of all the times it says "70%", the thing happens about 70% of the time.
calibration.coined: A core concept of forecast verification from meteorology; the calibration/reliability framing was systematized by Allan Murphy and co-workers in the 1970s — exact coinage not verified here.
calibration.intuition: A friend who says "I'm 90% sure" and is right half the time isn't lying about the world, they're lying about themselves. Calibration is self-knowledge: your confidence dial reads true. Note you can be perfectly calibrated and useless (always say the base rate) — you also need resolution/skill.
calibration.math: Perfect calibration: P(event | forecast = p) = p for all p. Diagnosed with reliability bins (btc_rl/metrics.py calibration_bins: mean stated p vs realized frequency per bucket) and repaired with Platt scaling.
calibration.here: The "Calibration honesty" section of metrics_lab.html (live Platt a·b per arm + three reliability buckets); btc_rl/agents.py PlattCalibrator does the repairing; sev0.html documents the tier-2 overconfidence defect it fixed.
calibration.code:
bins.append({"p_mean": mean(p), "y_freq": mean(y), "n": len(sel)})
# btc_rl/metrics.py calibration_bins — stated vs realized, 10 buckets

platt.what: A two-parameter repair for miscalibrated probabilities: learn (a, b) so that σ(a + b·logit(p)) is honest even when the model's raw p is not. a=0, b=1 is the identity ("already honest").
platt.coined: John Platt, 1999 ("Probabilistic outputs for support vector machines"), originally to turn SVM margins into probabilities; Guo et al. 2017 (ICML) showed modern neural nets need the same fix.
platt.intuition: Instead of retraining a bragging model, hire a tiny translator that learns the model's dialect: "when it says 90% it means 70%". b < 1 shrinks over-extreme claims toward 50% — exactly the correction our over-confident arms needed.
platt.math: p_cal = σ(a + b·logit(p_raw)) where logit(p) = log(p/(1−p)) and σ(z) = 1/(1+e^(−z)). (a, b) are fit by minimizing log loss on (stated p, outcome) pairs.
platt.here: btc_rl/agents.py PlattCalibrator — online, with a forgetting factor (decay 0.985) and damped Newton refits, because the miscalibration itself drifts (measured: kb went b 0.56 → 1.34 between history halves). Per-arm (a, b) shown on metrics_lab.html and sev0.html.
platt.code:
def predict(self, p):                      # btc_rl/agents.py PlattCalibrator
    return self._sig(self.a + self.b * self._logit(p))
platt.src: docs/RESEARCH_BASELINE.md 2.2/2.3 (Platt params used instead of ECE, per criticism literature)

conformal.what: A distribution-free way to build prediction intervals with a guaranteed hit rate: take the recent errors your model actually made, and use their quantiles as the band width.
conformal.coined: Developed by Gammerman, Vovk and colleagues in the late 1990s; the canonical book is Vovk, Gammerman & Shafer, "Algorithmic Learning in a Random World" (2005).
conformal.intuition: Don't trust the model's own opinion of its uncertainty — measure it. If your last 100 misses were mostly under $80, then "±$80-ish" is an evidence-based 80% band, no matter how the model works inside.
conformal.math: Band = prediction ± q̂, where q̂ is the 80th-percentile of recent |residuals|. Ours is normalized (volatility-conditioned): quantiles are taken over z = residual/σ_at_commit, then re-scaled by today's σ — so calm days get narrow bands and violent days wide ones.
conformal.here: btc_rl/online.py _band_map(): rolling 80% conformal band per arm x horizon (Papadopoulos-style locally-weighted scores; Lei et al. 2018). The 2026-08-28 fix replaced raw dollar quantiles (coverage 0.518 in violent regimes) with σ-normalized ones (0.868). Documented on sev0.html.
conformal.code:
z = residual / sigma_at_commit             # store z-scores, not dollars
band = pred +/- quantile(|z|, 0.8) * max(sigma_now, 0.6*median_sigma)

coverage.what: The fraction of times the true value actually landed inside the predicted band. An 80% band should cover about 80% of outcomes — more means the band is lazily wide, less means overconfident.
coverage.coined: From the coverage probability of confidence intervals (Neyman's 1937 interval-estimation theory); "PICP" (prediction interval coverage probability) is the forecasting literature's name — exact coinage not verified here.
coverage.intuition: A weather service whose "80% likely range" contains the real temperature only half the time is overpromising. But coverage alone is gameable — predict "between $0 and $1M" and you cover 100% — which is why pinball loss and sharpness ride alongside.
coverage.math: coverage = (# of outcomes inside [lo, hi]) / (# of bands issued), tracked per volatility regime here because a single aggregate can hide bad buckets (measured: calm 0.827 / violent 0.518 before the conformal fix).
coverage.here: band80_cov in scripts/run_audit.py tier1; per-regime coverage audit in btc_rl/online.py drove the 2026-08-28 band fix. On metrics_lab.html, live_online.html, home.html. Gap #8: track 50/80/95, not just 80.
coverage.code: cov = sum(1 for r in rows if r["lo"] <= r["actual"] <= r["hi"]) / len(rows)

sharpness.what: The average width of your prediction bands. Coverage's necessary companion: the goal is the narrowest band that still covers at the promised rate.
sharpness.coined: The principle "maximize sharpness subject to calibration" is due to Tilmann Gneiting and co-authors (mid-2000s probabilistic-forecasting program, e.g. Gneiting & Raftery 2007).
sharpness.intuition: Two forecasters both cover 80%. One says "between $109,900 and $110,100", the other "between $105,000 and $115,000". The first is doing real work; sharpness is the number that tells them apart.
sharpness.math: sharpness = mean(hi − lo) over all issued bands, in dollars. Read jointly with coverage: narrow + covering = skill; narrow + missing = overconfidence; wide + covering = laziness.
sharpness.here: btc_rl/metrics.py sharpness(); reported next to coverage for tier-1 bands (experiment_review.html).
sharpness.code:
def sharpness(los, his):                   # btc_rl/metrics.py
    return sum(h - l for l, h in zip(los, his)) / len(los)

sigma.what: The standard deviation of recent returns — the market's current "jumpiness". Everything in this stack that involves size or width is quoted in sigma units so it adapts to conditions.
sigma.coined: Karl Pearson coined "standard deviation" and the σ notation in the 1890s; volatility as the std of asset returns became central with Markowitz's portfolio theory (1952).
sigma.intuition: A $50 move at 3am on a dead Sunday is news; the same $50 during a CPI print is nothing. Dividing by sigma converts dollar moves into "how unusual is this, right now" — the honest unit.
sigma.math: σ = std of the last N one-minute returns, scaled to the horizon (σ_h ≈ σ_1m·√h). Used as: action bins in σ units (K_FACTORS), conformal band z = residual/σ, and regime buckets (calm/normal/elevated/violent).
sigma.here: Trailing sigma computed in btc_rl/features.py; K_FACTORS σ-scaled action bins in btc_rl/config.py and btc_rl/agents.py; σ-conditioned conformal bands in btc_rl/online.py _band_map. Regime tables on experiment_review.html and sev0.html.
sigma.code:
z = residual / sigma_at_commit             # conformal normalization
bins = K_FACTORS                            # action deltas in sigma units

z-score.what: A raw number re-expressed as "how many standard deviations from the norm": z = (x − mean)/σ. It puts everything on one universal scale.
z-score.coined: The standard score is early-20th-century statistics/psychometrics; exact attribution not verified here.
z-score.intuition: "Is $80 a big miss?" depends on the day. z = 0.5 says "routine"; z = 3 says "one of the largest misses we make" — regardless of whether the market is calm or wild. It's how the system compares errors across regimes fairly.
z-score.math: z = (x − μ)/σ. In the conformal band pipeline, residuals become z = residual/σ_at_commit, quantiles are taken in z-space, and bands are re-inflated by today's σ.
z-score.here: The tier-1 pipeline step "pred, σ → z-score" on sev0.html's architecture diagram; implemented inside btc_rl/online.py _band_map (normalized conformal scores).
z-score.code: z = (pred - actual) / sigma_at_commit      # store scale-free residuals

kelly.what: The bet-sizing formula that maximizes the long-run growth rate of a bankroll: bet a fraction of your money proportional to your edge, scaled by the odds.
kelly.coined: John L. Kelly Jr., 1956, "A New Interpretation of Information Rate" (Bell System Technical Journal) — derived at Bell Labs from information theory; famously used by Ed Thorp in blackjack and markets.
kelly.intuition: Bet too little and you waste your edge; bet too much and one bad streak ruins you even though you were right on average. Kelly is the exact middle: the fraction where compounding works hardest for you. Overbetting past Kelly actually lowers long-run growth.
kelly.math: For a binary bet at net odds b (win b per 1 staked): f* = (p·(1+b) − 1)/b, where p is your win probability. f* ≤ 0 means no edge — don't bet.
kelly.here: pt6 (the meta-trader logit) sizes with Kelly computed from its predicted P(win) and the actual Kalshi payout odds, then halves and caps it (btc_rl/online.py, ~line 3207). Discussed on home.html, ab_dashboard.html, sev0.html (Kelly 1956; MacLean, Thorp & Ziemba 2011 cited).
kelly.code:
odds = (100 - (askp + feep)) / (askp + feep)    # btc_rl/online.py
kelly = max(0.0, (pw6 * (1 + odds) - 1) / odds)
frac = min(0.10, 0.5 * kelly)                    # half-Kelly, 10% cap
kelly.src: docs/RESEARCH_BASELINE.md 3.5 (Kelly-fraction sizing under estimation error, MacLean-Thorp-Ziemba)

half-kelly.what: Betting half of the full Kelly fraction. Costs only ~25% of the theoretical growth rate but cuts the swings roughly in half — the practitioner's standard hedge against overestimating your own edge.
half-kelly.coined: Fractional-Kelly practice grew among gamblers and quant investors (Thorp among them); analyzed formally in MacLean, Thorp & Ziemba's work on fractional Kelly strategies (2011 volume).
half-kelly.intuition: Full Kelly assumes your probability estimate is exactly right. It never is. If your true edge is smaller than you think, full Kelly is over-betting — the ruinous side of the curve. Halving is cheap insurance against your own overconfidence.
half-kelly.math: f = 0.5 · f*_Kelly. Growth is roughly quadratic near the optimum, so betting half the fraction keeps about three-quarters of the growth with far less variance and drawdown.
half-kelly.here: pt6's sizing rule: frac = min(0.10, 0.5 * kelly) — half-Kelly with a hard 10%-of-bankroll cap (btc_rl/online.py). Explained on home.html and sev0.html.
half-kelly.code:
frac = min(0.10, 0.5 * kelly)              # half-Kelly, capped at 10%
cap = min(int(frac * pt6_bankroll_c), dcap)

drawdown.what: The largest peak-to-trough fall of the cumulative P&L curve — the worst "how much did I give back from my high point" experience over the period.
drawdown.coined: Origin: trading and fund-performance practice; exact attribution not verified here.
drawdown.intuition: Average return hides pain. A strategy that ends up +$50 after being down $400 mid-way is very different from one that never dipped below −$20. Drawdown is the number your stomach cares about — and the denominator that makes returns comparable.
drawdown.math: MDD = max over time of (running_peak − current_value). Computed by one pass: track the peak, record the deepest gap below it.
drawdown.here: btc_rl/metrics.py max_drawdown() on the bankroll curve; scripts/run_audit.py reports it per trader; the scoreboard ranks traders by net ÷ DD (NOTES TA-feedback entry). On home.html, ab_dashboard.html, experiment_review.html.
drawdown.code:
for v in cum:                              # btc_rl/metrics.py max_drawdown
    peak = max(peak, v)
    worst = max(worst, peak - v)

ev.what: The probability-weighted average outcome of a bet: what you'd earn per bet if you could replay it many times. This project's universal money metric is EV per $1 staked.
ev.coined: The concept comes from the 1654 Pascal-Fermat correspondence on gambling problems; Christiaan Huygens wrote the first treatise on expectation (1657).
ev.intuition: One bet's result is luck; the average over a thousand replays is skill. A bet with EV +$0.03 per $1 loses often — but making it every day is a business, while a −EV bet made every day is a leak, even when it wins tonight.
ev.math: EV = Σ p(outcome)·value(outcome). For one settled Kalshi bet at total cost c cents: EV/$1 = (100 − c)/c if won, −1 if lost (bet_ev in treatments.py).
ev.here: EV/$1 is the shared currency of every layer: bet_ev() in btc_rl/treatments.py, EV/$1 per trader in scripts/run_audit.py, SPRT's pre-registered edge is 0.02 EV/$1. Everywhere on home.html, ab_dashboard.html, live_online.html, metrics_lab.html.
ev.code:
def bet_ev(side, ask_c, outcome):          # btc_rl/treatments.py
    cost = ask_c + fee
    won = (side == "yes") == bool(outcome)
    return (100.0 - cost) / cost if won else -1.0

break-even.what: The win rate (or price) at which a strategy makes exactly zero. Buying a YES at 62c + 2c fee needs the event to happen more than 64% of the time to profit.
break-even.coined: From business break-even analysis (accounting practice); exact attribution not verified here.
break-even.intuition: "We win 58% of our bets!" means nothing until you know the price paid. At 50c that's a money machine; at 62c it's a slow leak. Break-even is the bar the price itself sets — skill only counts above it.
break-even.math: break_even = (ask + fee)/100 as a probability. Profit requires P(win) > break_even; the edge is the gap between your true win rate and this bar.
break-even.here: scripts/run_audit.py computes break_even_pct per day and per trader and compares the realized win% against the break-even actually paid (not a fixed 50%). Shown on home.html, live_online.html, sev0.html.
break-even.code:
be_pct = (avg_ask_c + avg_fee_c)           # scripts/run_audit.py
edge = win_pct - be_pct                     # skill is the gap, not raw win%

sprt.what: A statistical test you can watch continuously: evidence accumulates as a running log-likelihood ratio, and the test ends the moment it crosses a pre-set "promote" or "reject" boundary — no fixed sample size.
sprt.coined: Abraham Wald, 1945 (developed for WWII munitions quality control; published in Annals of Mathematical Statistics, book "Sequential Analysis" 1947). Proven optimal: it needs the fewest samples on average for given error rates.
sprt.intuition: Classic tests forbid peeking — check your p-value every day and your false-positive rate explodes. SPRT is built for peeking: the boundaries already account for continuous watching, which is exactly how a live trading desk behaves.
sprt.math: Accumulate LLR = Σ log[P(data|H1)/P(data|H0)]. Promote when LLR ≥ log((1−β)/α); reject when LLR ≤ log(β/(1−α)). Here H0: paired difference = 0, H1: difference = 0.02 EV/$1 (pre-registered).
sprt.here: btc_rl/treatments.py class SPRT — the promotion engine of the treatment board, with Welford online variance, a variance floor (a measured LLR-123 false-promotion incident forced it), warmup 12, min_n 40, and Bonferroni-split α. Live boundaries on board.html and metrics_lab.html.
sprt.code:
s2 = max(self.var(), self.VAR_FLOOR)       # btc_rl/treatments.py SPRT.add
self.llr += (self.edge * (d - self.edge/2.0)) / s2
# verdict: llr >= log((1-beta)/alpha) -> promote

llr.what: The running evidence score of a sequential test: log of "how much more likely is this data under the challenger-wins hypothesis than under no-difference". Positive favors the challenger; it adds up one observation at a time.
llr.coined: Likelihood-ratio testing is Neyman & Pearson, 1933 ("On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses") — their lemma says the likelihood ratio is the most powerful possible test statistic.
llr.intuition: Each settled window is a clue. A window where the challenger beat the champion nudges the score up; a losing window nudges it down; the size of the nudge depends on how surprising the clue is. Enough consistent clues push the score over the promotion line.
llr.math: Per observation d (challenger − champion EV), under the normal plug-in: ΔLLR = edge·(d − edge/2)/s², where s² is the running variance (floored). Boundaries: log((1−β)/α) above, log(β/(1−α)) below.
llr.here: SPRT.llr in btc_rl/treatments.py; every treatment's live LLR, boundary, and progress bar are on board.html and metrics_lab.html (boundaries moved when α was Bonferroni-corrected: 2.89 → 5.66).

alpha-beta.what: The two ways a statistical test can fail: α is the chance of promoting a dud (false positive, Type I); β is the chance of missing a real winner (false negative, Type II). You choose both in advance and the test's boundaries follow.
alpha-beta.coined: Jerzy Neyman & Egon Pearson introduced the two error types in their 1928-1933 papers founding modern hypothesis testing.
alpha-beta.intuition: A smoke alarm has the same dilemma: too sensitive and it screams at toast (α), too lazy and it sleeps through a fire (β). You cannot make both zero with finite data — you pick your poison rates and buy enough data to honor them. Watch out: the same Greek letters are reused elsewhere (LinUCB's exploration width, Fixed-Share's share rate) — context decides.
alpha-beta.math: In the SPRT the pair sets the boundaries directly: upper = log((1−β)/α), lower = log(β/(1−α)). Ours: α = 0.05/16 (family-wise split), β = 0.10.
alpha-beta.here: SPRT(alpha, beta) in btc_rl/treatments.py; TREAT_ALPHA = 0.05/TREAT_MAX_CONCURRENT in btc_rl/online.py. The α-correction and boundary move are annotated on board.html and metrics_lab.html.
alpha-beta.code:
self.alpha = alpha   # P(promote a dud)      treatments.py SPRT
self.beta = beta     # P(miss a real win)
upper = math.log((1 - beta) / alpha)

bonferroni.what: When you run many tests at once, the chance that at least one lies to you (the family-wise error rate) balloons. The Bonferroni correction divides your α budget by the number of tests so the family as a whole stays honest.
bonferroni.coined: Named for Carlo Emilio Bonferroni's probability inequalities (1936); its use as a multiple-comparisons correction was formalized by Olive Jean Dunn (1961).
bonferroni.intuition: Roll a 20-sided die once and a 1 is rare. Roll it 14 times and a 1 somewhere is likely. Fourteen concurrent treatments each tested at 5% means a false "winner" is practically guaranteed eventually — and we promote the best-looking one, the exact trap.
bonferroni.math: α_each = α_family / m. Here: 0.05/16 = 0.003125 per treatment (m = registered concurrency cap, not current count — so boundaries are pre-set). SPRT upper boundary moved log(0.9/0.003125) ≈ 5.66, from 2.89.
bonferroni.here: btc_rl/online.py TREAT_ALPHA = 0.05 / TREAT_MAX_CONCURRENT (2026-08-28, research-baseline gap #1 closed after two near-miss false promotions). Annotated on board.html and metrics_lab.html ("family-wise α-corrected" boundaries).
bonferroni.code:
TREAT_MAX_CONCURRENT = 16                  # registered cap, btc_rl/online.py
TREAT_ALPHA = 0.05 / TREAT_MAX_CONCURRENT  # 0.003125 per treatment

ab-test.what: Run two versions at the same time on comparable traffic, measure the same outcome, and let the difference — not opinions — decide. The randomized controlled trial, applied to product and strategy changes.
ab-test.coined: The underlying method is R. A. Fisher's randomized experiments (1920s Rothamsted; "The Design of Experiments", 1935). The name "A/B test" comes from the web-experimentation era (2000s); exact coinage not verified here.
ab-test.intuition: Comparing this week's new model against last week's old one confounds the change with the market's mood. Running both on the same windows makes the market's mood cancel out — the only remaining difference is the thing you changed.
ab-test.math: Effect = mean(outcome_B − outcome_A) on paired units, with a significance rule sized to α and β. Ours is sequential (SPRT) rather than fixed-horizon because the desk is monitored continuously.
ab-test.here: The whole treatment board (btc_rl/treatments.py + btc_rl/online.py): every change ships as a challenger paired against the champion on identical live windows. ab_dashboard.html is the dedicated page; results also on metrics_lab.html and home.html.
ab-test.code:
d = own_ev - champ_ev                      # same window, same outcome
self.sprt.add(d)                           # sequential A/B, treatments.py
ab-test.src: Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (docs/RESEARCH_BASELINE.md 4.2)

treatment-control.what: Experiment vocabulary: the treatment is the thing you changed; the control is the untouched twin that shows what would have happened anyway. Only the difference between them is evidence.
treatment-control.coined: From R. A. Fisher's agricultural experiments at Rothamsted (1920s; "The Design of Experiments", 1935) — the original treatments were literally fertilizers on crop plots.
treatment-control.intuition: If you take medicine and feel better, maybe the cold just passed. The control group catches the "would have happened anyway" — in our case a raging bull market that makes every strategy look like a genius until you subtract the twin that did nothing different.
treatment-control.math: Effect = outcome(treatment) − outcome(control), on paired windows so shared noise cancels. A baseline treatment paired against itself gets no verdict by design (d ≡ 0 would otherwise drift to REJECT — measured LLR −2.80).
treatment-control.here: class Treatment in btc_rl/treatments.py; every candidate change (M2 knife veto, M8 regime gate, M11 maker limit...) runs as one. Live table on ab_dashboard.html, board.html, metrics_lab.html; the Follower control appears on sev0.html.

champion-challenger.what: A promotion discipline: the champion is the strategy currently in charge; challengers run alongside it and one takes over only by beating the champion significantly on live data. The loser keeps running so a regression stays visible.
champion-challenger.coined: Industry practice from credit scoring and direct marketing (champion/challenger model management); exact attribution not verified here.
champion-challenger.intuition: Like a boxing title: you don't become champion by looking good in the gym (backtests) — you must beat the current champion in a real fight, with judges (the SPRT) and pre-agreed scoring. And the belt can be taken back.
champion-challenger.math: Challenger promoted when its paired-difference SPRT crosses the upper boundary: LLR ≥ log((1−β)/α) with α family-wise corrected. Promotion is stamped (timestamp recorded) and reversible.
champion-challenger.here: btc_rl/treatments.py (promote() stamps promoted_at; the loser is retained, not deleted). The router in btc_rl/online.py sends live decisions through the current champion. Status on board.html, metrics_lab.html, sev0.html.
champion-challenger.code:
def promote(t):                            # btc_rl/treatments.py
    t.promoted_at = int(time.time())       # stamped, reversible

paired.what: Scoring two strategies on the identical situations and analyzing the per-situation differences, instead of comparing their separate averages. Shared noise subtracts away, leaving a much cleaner signal.
paired.coined: The paired-comparison t-test lineage begins with "Student" (W. S. Gosset), 1908, "The probable error of a mean" (Biometrika).
paired.intuition: To compare two runners, race them on the same track on the same day — don't compare one's rainy-day time with the other's sunny-day time. On 08/27 a single regime day was enough to swamp an unpaired comparison entirely; pairing made it cancel.
paired.math: d_i = score_B(window_i) − score_A(window_i); test mean(d) against 0. Crucially, effective n = number of windows, not rows — entries inside one 15-minute window share one outcome and must not be counted twice.
paired.here: The core design rule of btc_rl/treatments.py (header: "PAIRED, same-window comparison") and of Method A's market-paired scoring (win − q with day-clustered t). Explained on ab_dashboard.html, board.html, metrics_lab.html.
paired.code:
d = own_ev - champ_ev    # same window, same settled outcome
# regime cancels out of d; effective n = windows, not rows

prequential.what: Test-then-train: every prediction is scored on data the model had never seen, then the model may learn from it. The evaluation IS the live sequence — no train/test split to get wrong.
prequential.coined: A. Philip Dawid, 1984 ("Present position and potential developments: … the prequential approach", JRSS A) — a portmanteau of "predictive" + "sequential".
prequential.intuition: The strictest exam possible: the model states tomorrow's forecast today, gets graded on the real tomorrow, and only then gets to study that day. Nothing can leak from the future because the future hadn't happened when the forecast was locked.
prequential.math: Score = Σ loss(prediction_t made before t, outcome_t), with model updates allowed only after scoring. Our decayed prequential log-loss compares calibrated vs raw probabilities on this schedule.
prequential.here: The project's primary evaluation discipline (docs/RESEARCH_BASELINE.md 3.4: "does by a stronger route" than purged CV). PlattCalibrator's scoreboard in btc_rl/agents.py is prequential (Dawid 1984 cited in code); mentioned on metrics_lab.html and sev0.html.
prequential.code:
p_cal = calib.predict(p_raw)   # 1. predict (frozen)
score(p_cal, outcome)          # 2. test
calib.update(p_raw, outcome)   # 3. only then train

leakage.what: When information from the future (or from the answer itself) sneaks into a model's inputs or evaluation, producing performance that evaporates in live trading. The #1 killer of financial ML results.
leakage.coined: The term is ML-practice vernacular; formalized by Kaufman, Rosset & Perlich ("Leakage in data mining", c. 2011). In finance, López de Prado's purged/embargoed CV is the standard countermeasure.
leakage.intuition: Grading yesterday's weather forecast using today's newspaper is easy. Subtle versions are deadly: a feature computed over a window that ends after the prediction time, or overlapping labels sharing a future bar. The backtest shines; the live desk bleeds.
leakage.math: No formula — an invariant: every input to a prediction at time t must be measurable strictly before t, and every score must use only the outcome after t. Overlapping labels additionally require purging/embargo in any CV split.
leakage.here: btc_rl/features.py builds features with explicit no-look-ahead; replays recompute signals under the same rule (Method B); kb9's fine-tune trained strictly before its eval cutoff; t_cal scores from pre-settle stamps (fix #3). Called out on experiment_review.html, index.html, metrics_lab.html.

adverse-selection.what: The counterparty who accepts your order knows something you don't — so you get filled most easily exactly when you're wrong. Passive orders are systematically "picked off" by better-informed traders.
adverse-selection.coined: From insurance economics (the sick buy more insurance); the canonical formalization is George Akerlof's "The Market for 'Lemons'" (1970, QJE) — the term itself predates it in the insurance literature.
adverse-selection.intuition: You offer to buy YES at 85c. Who sells to you? Disproportionately, people who just saw the price start falling. Your order is a free option for the informed: they trade when you're wrong, walk away when you're right. Measured here: at the 0.85 tail, half our maker fills were exactly these poisoned fills.
adverse-selection.math: E[outcome | your order filled] < E[outcome | order placed] — conditioning on being filled worsens the bet. The fix is measuring edge at the fill, not at the decision (and gap #10: post-fill markouts).
adverse-selection.here: The measured 0.85-tail adverse selection (50%) in docs/SEV0_REMEDIATION.md Tier 3; drives the maker-vs-taker treatments (M11 t_limit) and M10 fill-quality guard in btc_rl/online.py. Explained on home.html ("the market prices out the good calls"), ab_dashboard.html, sev0.html.

# decision-time quote by > threshold (worst 10% of fills = the poison)

maker-taker.what: Two ways to trade: a maker posts a resting limit order and waits (adds liquidity); a taker crosses the spread and trades instantly against a resting order (removes liquidity). Makers pay less but wait and risk adverse selection; takers pay the spread for certainty.
maker-taker.coined: The maker/taker terminology comes from electronic exchange fee schedules of the late-1990s/2000s ECN era; exact attribution not verified here.
maker-taker.intuition: At a market stall: the maker puts up a sign "I'll buy at 60c" and waits; the taker walks up and pays the seller's asking price now. The maker saves cents but might only get filled when the deal has gone sour — that trade-off is measurable, and we measured it.
maker-taker.math: Maker saves ≈ spread but E[fill] is adversely selected; taker pays spread but chooses the moment. Measured here: maker-style entries −10.6c/contract without speed advantages; late taker entries +9.1c.
maker-taker.here: The maker-vs-taker experiments in docs/SEV0_REMEDIATION.md ("Ideal trader"); M11 t_limit maker treatment in btc_rl/online.py (rest 2c below, fill or skip); pt8's 25% participation cap. Discussed on home.html, ab_dashboard.html, metrics_lab.html, sev0.html.

# btc_rl/online.py treatment registry

limit-order.what: An order with a price condition: "buy, but only at 60c or better". It rests in the order book until someone accepts your price — or never fills at all. The opposite of a market order, which takes whatever price is available now.
limit-order.coined: Exchange practice dating to 19th-century stock exchanges; exact attribution not verified here.
limit-order.intuition: It's a standing offer, not a purchase. You control the price but surrender control of the timing and the certainty — the market decides if and when your offer is hit, and (see adverse selection) it tends to hit you at the worst times.
limit-order.math: Fill is an option held by the counterparty: you receive price improvement ≈ spread when filled, times P(fill), minus the adverse-selection cost E[loss | filled]. Whether that nets positive is an empirical question — ours is the M11 treatment.
limit-order.here: The t_limit treatment in btc_rl/online.py: rest a bid 2c below the quote, trade only if filled, skip otherwise (skips score EV 0 — standing down is a real decision). On ab_dashboard.html, home.html, metrics_lab.html.

slippage.what: The gap between the price you decided to trade at and the price you actually got. Individually tiny, collectively it can eat an entire edge.
slippage.coined: Trading-floor vernacular; exact attribution not verified here. Its formal umbrella is implementation shortfall (Perold, 1988).
slippage.intuition: You decide to buy at 62c; by the time the order lands, it costs 65c. Three cents on a 3-cent edge is 100% of the profit. Measured on this desk: execution cost 2.70 points of EV (real fills −9.73% vs decision-time quotes −7.02%) — more than double the best treatment's edge.
slippage.math: slippage = fill_price − decision_price (per side). Aggregated with delay and unfilled-opportunity cost it becomes implementation shortfall vs the arrival price (gap #6).
slippage.here: The M10 guard in btc_rl/online.py declines fills worse than the decision-time quote beyond a threshold; the 2.1c pricing-bug fix made every policy price from the same decision-time quote (arrival-price convention). Numbers on sev0.html and metrics_lab.html.

market-maker.what: A participant who continuously quotes both a buy (bid) and a sell (ask) price, earning the spread between them in exchange for always being available to trade — and managing the risk of being run over by informed flow.
market-maker.coined: From exchange floor practice (specialists on the NYSE, jobbers in London); exact attribution not verified here.
market-maker.intuition: The currency-exchange booth at the airport: it will always buy your euros a bit low and sell them a bit high. The spread pays for the service — and for the danger that the person trading with them knows something (adverse selection is the market maker's tax).
market-maker.math: Earns spread x volume, loses to informed flow: profit ≈ spread·uninformed_volume − adverse_selection_cost·informed_volume. Detection of a consistently winning counterparty makes them widen or pull quotes.
market-maker.here: The counterparty on every Kalshi book we trade against. home.html's capacity study simulates makers detecting a winner ("market makers quote a detected winner's edge away in days") — the reason pt8 caps participation at 25% of near-touch size.

ofi.what: A measure of buying vs selling pressure read from the order book: are bids stacking up and asks thinning (buyers pressing), or the reverse? One of the few reliable very-short-horizon predictors.
ofi.coined: Order-book pressure measures are as old as electronic books; the specific OFI formulation was formalized by Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov ("The price impact of order book events", 2014).
ofi.intuition: Watch a queue at two doors: if the "buy" line grows while the "sell" line shrinks, the price is about to get pushed up — not because of news, but because of simple pressure. It fades fast, which is why it only helps the shortest horizons.
ofi.math: Simplest book form (ours): imbalance = (bid_sz − ask_sz)/(bid_sz + ask_sz) in [−1, +1]. Cont et al.'s event version sums signed size changes at the best quotes; price impact is near-linear in OFI.
ofi.here: Computed from the Kalshi book in btc_rl/features.py (top-of-book sizes via btc_rl/sources.py) and fed to the tier-1 contextual arms and tier-2 features. Referenced on experiment_review.html, live_online.html, sev0.html.
ofi.code: imb = (bid_sz - ask_sz) / max(1, bid_sz + ask_sz)   # btc_rl/features.py

linucb.what: A contextual bandit algorithm: each action keeps a linear (ridge regression) model of reward, and you pick the action with the best optimistic estimate — predicted reward plus an uncertainty bonus. "Optimism in the face of uncertainty."
linucb.coined: Li, Chu, Langford & Schapire, 2010 ("A contextual-bandit approach to personalized news article recommendation", WWW) — built for Yahoo!'s front-page news module. The UCB principle it extends: Lai & Robbins (1985), UCB1 by Auer, Cesa-Bianchi & Fischer (2002).
linucb.intuition: Restaurant choice with a twist: order the dish that's either provably great OR insufficiently tried. The uncertainty bonus shrinks as an arm gets data, so exploration is automatic, targeted, and fades exactly where knowledge grows.
linucb.math: Choose a = argmax_a [θ_aᵀx + α·sqrt(xᵀA_a⁻¹x)] where A_a = λI + Σxxᵀ (ridge design matrix), θ_a = A_a⁻¹b_a, and the sqrt term is the width of the confidence ellipsoid along x.
linucb.here: btc_rl/agents.py class LinUCBAgent — the tier-1 workhorse (arms t2, t6, t10, t11 across horizons; state in results/linucb_t*-h*.json). Purely online, no batch retrain; pad_to() grows the context without losing learned statistics. On live_online.html, experiment_review.html, sev0.html.
linucb.code:
p = theta @ x + self.alpha * math.sqrt(x @ Ainv @ x)   # optimism
# A_a = lam*I + sum(x xT); b_a += r*x     btc_rl/agents.py LinUCBAgent

bandit.what: A learning problem where you repeatedly pick one of several actions (arms), see the reward of only the arm you picked, and must balance exploring (learning about arms) against exploiting (playing the best-known arm). "Contextual" = you also see features before choosing.
bandit.coined: "One-armed bandit" is slot-machine slang; the formal problem is Herbert Robbins (1952, "Some aspects of the sequential design of experiments"). The contextual variant was named in the 2000s learning-theory literature (Langford & Zhang, 2008); exact coinage not verified here.
bandit.intuition: Ten slot machines, unknown payouts, limited coins. Play only your favorite and you may never discover the best; sample all forever and you waste coins on duds. Every ad server, news feed and — here — action-picker faces this dilemma.
bandit.math: Each round: observe context x, choose arm a, observe reward r(a) only. Goal: minimize regret vs always playing the best arm. Our tier-1 pickers are one-step bandits (no state transition), so Q-learning here needs no bootstrapping.
bandit.here: The frame for all tier-1 action-pickers (btc_rl/agents.py: LinUCB, LinearQ, tabular Q over σ-scaled delta arms). Deliberately NOT used for arm selection in tier 2: we see every arm's outcome each window (full information), so Fixed-Share expert advice is used instead (btc_rl/treatments.py rationale).

q-learning.what: Learning a table of Q(state, action) values — "how good is doing this in this situation" — by nudging each entry toward the rewards actually received. Pick actions by reading the best row entry.
q-learning.coined: Chris Watkins, 1989 PhD thesis ("Learning from Delayed Rewards", Cambridge); convergence proof Watkins & Dayan, 1992. The "Q" stands for the quality of a state-action pair.
q-learning.intuition: A notebook: rows are situations ("calm market, price above strike"), columns are moves, cells hold a running average of how each move worked out. Every outcome updates one cell a little. No model of the world needed — just bookkeeping that slowly becomes wisdom.
q-learning.math: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α·(target − Q(s,a)). Ours is one-step (a contextual bandit, so target = r, no bootstrapped max-over-next-state term): Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α·(r − Q(s,a)), with ε-greedy exploration.
q-learning.here: btc_rl/agents.py class TabularQAgent (Level 1) over discretized states and σ-scaled delta arms; live state in results/q_table_online_h{5,15,30}.json. On live_training.html, live_online.html, index.html, metrics_lab.html.
q-learning.code:
q = self.q[state][action_idx]              # btc_rl/agents.py TabularQAgent
self.q[state][action_idx] = q + config.ALPHA * (r - q)

dqn.what: Q-learning with a neural network instead of a table: the network maps a situation to values (here, a distribution) over actions, so similar situations share learning instead of each needing its own table row.
dqn.coined: Mnih et al. (DeepMind), 2013 arXiv / 2015 Nature ("Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning") — the Atari-from-pixels result that launched deep RL.
dqn.intuition: A table needs to have visited YOUR exact situation before; a network generalizes — "this is like those other volatile afternoons". The price is stability: networks can chase their own errors, which is why ours predicts a full distribution and trains on realized outcomes only (no bootstrapping).
dqn.math: Ours (t8) is a distributional variant: an MLP maps context to a categorical distribution over σ-scaled delta bins, trained by cross-entropy against the realized bin; greedy action = the distribution's mode.
dqn.here: btc_rl/agents.py class DistDQNAgent (Level 3, arm t8; weights in results/dqn_t8-h*.pt; offline warm-start scripts/train_l3.py). Support includes overflow bins (±2σ, ±3σ) — without them clipped tail mass made the mode degenerate into a permanent ±1.5σ bet. On live_training.html, live_online.html, sev0.html.
dqn.code:
dist = softmax(mlp(x))                     # over sigma-scaled bins
loss = cross_entropy(dist, realized_bin)   # act on the mode

distributional-rl.what: Instead of learning the average outcome of an action, learn the whole probability distribution of outcomes. The average hides everything risk cares about.
distributional-rl.coined: Bellemare, Dabney & Munos, 2017 ("A Distributional Perspective on Reinforcement Learning", ICML — the C51 algorithm), building on older risk-sensitive RL threads.
distributional-rl.intuition: Two bets both average +$1: one is "always win $1", the other "win $101 or lose $99, coin flip". Identical to a mean-learner, wildly different to anyone with a bankroll. Keeping the distribution keeps that difference — and gives a mode, quantiles, and tail mass to act on.
distributional-rl.math: Learn p(z | s, a) over a discrete support of outcome bins rather than E[z | s, a]. Ours: categorical distribution over σ-scaled delta bins (K_FACTORS + overflow bins), cross-entropy loss against the realized bin, one-step targets.
distributional-rl.here: Both deep tier-1 arms are distributional: DistDQNAgent (t8) and LSTMDistAgent (t9) in btc_rl/agents.py predict the delta distribution and act on its mode. On live_training.html, experiment_review.html, index.html.
distributional-rl.code:
self.bins = sorted(set(config.K_FACTORS) | {2.0,-2.0,3.0,-3.0})
# overflow bins stop tail mass from piling onto the +/-1.5 edges

lstm.what: Long Short-Term Memory — a recurrent neural network with learnable gates that decide what to remember and what to forget, letting it hold information across long sequences without the signal dying out.
lstm.coined: Sepp Hochreiter & Jürgen Schmidhuber, 1997 (Neural Computation). It solved the vanishing-gradient problem that crippled earlier recurrent nets, and powered speech/translation systems through the 2010s.
lstm.intuition: Reading a sentence, you carry forward what matters ("the subject was plural") and drop what doesn't. An LSTM has trainable little doors — input, forget, output gates — that learn that skill for any sequence, here the minute-by-minute rhythm of prices.
lstm.math: Per step: forget gate f_t = σ(W_f·[h_{t−1},x_t]), input gate i_t, output gate o_t; cell state c_t = f_t∘c_{t−1} + i_t∘tanh(...); hidden h_t = o_t∘tanh(c_t). The cell state c is the protected memory line.
lstm.here: btc_rl/agents.py class LSTMDistAgent (Level 4, arm t9): nn.LSTM(1, 32) over the raw 1-minute return stream, predicting the same σ-scaled delta distribution as t8 and acting on its mode. Weights results/lstm_t9-h*.pt; warm-start scripts/train_l4.py. On live_training.html, live_online.html.

self.lstm = nn.LSTM(1, 32, batch_first=True)   # agents.py LSTMDistAgent
y = self.head(out[:, -1])                      # last step -> bin logits

chronos.what: Amazon's pretrained time-series foundation model: it treats a numeric series like a sentence (values quantized into tokens) and forecasts zero-shot — no training on your data. Chronos-Bolt is the faster direct-multi-step variant.
chronos.coined: Ansari et al. (Amazon), 2024 — "Chronos: Learning the Language of Time Series". Pretrained on a large corpus of public time series.
chronos.intuition: Like asking a well-read stranger to continue a melody: it has heard millions of tunes, so it continues yours plausibly without knowing the instrument. The open question this project tests: does having "read everything" beat tiny models that only know BTC? (Tier-1 finding so far: nothing beats persistence by much.)
chronos.math: Series → scaled & quantized tokens → transformer predicts token distribution → sampled trajectories give quantiles. We convert its trajectory samples into P(price > strike) by counting sample paths above the strike.
chronos.here: btc_rl/online.py _chronos_p_up() loads amazon/chronos-bolt-small (CPU) and turns 1-minute closes + strike into a probability — a zero-shot foundation-model arm beside the trained ones. On ab_dashboard.html, home.html, live_online.html, sev0.html.

pipe = BaseChronosPipeline.from_pretrained(
