timesfm.what: Google Research's time-series foundation model: a decoder-only transformer (GPT-style, but over patches of numbers instead of words) pretrained on billions of time points, forecasting zero-shot.
timesfm.coined: Das et al. (Google Research), 2024 — "A decoder-only foundation model for time-series forecasting" (ICML 2024). We use the timesfm-2.5 200M-parameter checkpoint.
timesfm.intuition: Same bet as Chronos from a different lab: maybe patterns learned across electricity demand, traffic and retail transfer to 30 minutes of Bitcoin. Running both here answers whether "general pattern knowledge" carries any edge over the naive floor in this market.
timesfm.math: Input patches → decoder-only transformer → output patches of future values with quantile heads. We read its quantile forecast at the horizon and convert to P(price > strike).
timesfm.here: btc_rl/online.py _timesfm_p_up() loads google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch; runs as a zero-shot arm beside Chronos. On ab_dashboard.html, home.html, live_online.html, sev0.html.

foundation-model.what: A large model pretrained once on broad data, then applied (often zero-shot, without retraining) to many downstream tasks. GPT for text, Chronos/TimesFM for time series.
foundation-model.coined: Term coined by Stanford's Center for Research on Foundation Models — Bommasani et al., 2021, "On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models".
foundation-model.intuition: Instead of teaching a new student per task, educate one polymath and hand them each task cold. The bet is that breadth transfers. This project runs that bet head-to-head: polymaths (Chronos, TimesFM) vs specialists (LinUCB, DQN, LSTM trained only on BTC) vs doing nothing (persistence) — on live money-metrics.
foundation-model.math: Not a formula but a recipe: pretrain on massive diverse corpora with self-supervised objectives; deploy with frozen weights. Zero-shot means our BTC stream never updates them — pure transfer.
foundation-model.here: The foundation-model arms are _chronos_p_up and _timesfm_p_up in btc_rl/online.py; the A/B against trained/naive arms is on ab_dashboard.html and home.html.
foundation-model.code:
# zero-shot: pretrained weights, frozen; our data only at inference
p_up = count(samples > strike) / n_samples

logistic.what: The workhorse model for probabilities: a weighted sum of features squashed through the S-shaped sigmoid to land in (0,1). "Logit" is the inverse squash — it maps a probability back to an unbounded score.
logistic.coined: The logistic function: Pierre-François Verhulst, 1838-1845 (population growth). The term "logit": Joseph Berkson, 1944. Logistic regression became the standard probability model in statistics through the mid-20th century.
logistic.intuition: Each feature pushes a lever up or down ("price above strike: +2", "volatile: −1"); the sigmoid converts the total push into a probability that saturates sensibly — huge evidence gets you 0.999, not 1.7. Every weight is readable, which is why our most-trusted arms are logits.
logistic.math: p = σ(w·x + b), σ(z) = 1/(1+e^(−z)); logit(p) = log(p/(1−p)) = w·x + b. Trained online here by SGD on log loss — each settled window nudges the weights.
logistic.here: The tier-2 kb arms are online logits (kb3 24 features, kb4 stacker, kb5, kb8 log-opinion pool — results/kb*_logit.json, dissected weight-by-weight in docs/MODEL_INTERNALS.md §1), and pt6 the meta-trader logit. Platt scaling operates in logit space. On metrics_lab.html, live_online.html, sev0.html, ab_dashboard.html.
logistic.code:
z = b + sum(w_i * x_i for ...)             # kb arm, btc_rl/online.py
p_up = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-z))          # then Platt-calibrated

fixed-share.what: An expert-tracking algorithm: keep a weight per expert (arm), multiply weights by performance each round — then redistribute a fixed share of all weight uniformly. That leak is the point: it tracks the best SEQUENCE of experts, not the best single one.
fixed-share.coined: Mark Herbster & Manfred Warmuth, 1998 — "Tracking the best expert" (Machine Learning). A classic of online learning theory.
fixed-share.intuition: Pure winner-take-all buries an arm that had one bad week — forever. The share step keeps every arm on life support, so when the regime turns, yesterday's loser can recover fast. Chosen from measurement: kb4 was the best arm (+4.7%/$1) on 08/27 and underwater (−3.7%) one day later. A frozen winner is a losing policy in this market.
fixed-share.math: w_a ∝ w_a·exp(−η·loss_a), normalize, then w_a ← (1−α)·w_a + α/K. η = 1.2 (learning rate on log loss), α = 0.08 (share), K = number of arms.
fixed-share.here: btc_rl/treatments.py class FixedShare, weighting the kb arms by per-window log loss. Chosen over a bandit deliberately: every arm's outcome is observed every window (full information), so exploration would waste data. On sev0.html.
fixed-share.code:
self.w[a] *= math.exp(-self.eta * loss)    # treatments.py FixedShare
self.w[a] = (1-self.alpha)*self.w[a] + self.alpha/k   # the share step

diebold-mariano.what: The standard statistical test for "is forecaster A actually more accurate than forecaster B, or is the gap luck?" — built on the time series of their per-period loss differences, with autocorrelation handled.
diebold-mariano.coined: Francis Diebold & Roberto Mariano, 1995 — "Comparing Predictive Accuracy" (Journal of Business & Economic Statistics).
diebold-mariano.intuition: Don't compare two averages and squint. Take the difference in loss on every single period — a paired series — and ask if its mean is distinguishable from zero, remembering that consecutive periods aren't independent (a windy week moves both forecasters together).
diebold-mariano.math: d_t = loss_A(t) − loss_B(t); DM = mean(d)/sqrt(LRV(d)/n), where LRV is a long-run (autocorrelation-consistent) variance. Approximately N(0,1) under the null of equal accuracy.
diebold-mariano.here: Cited in btc_rl/treatments.py's design references — the paired same-window scoring with day-clustered errors (Method A) is this test's discipline applied to the arm comparisons. Referenced on ab_dashboard.html, experiment_review.html, live_online.html, sev0.html.
diebold-mariano.code:
d_t = loss_A[t] - loss_B[t]                # paired loss differences
# test mean(d) with autocorrelation-robust (day-clustered) variance

meta-labeling.what: A two-model design: the primary model decides the DIRECTION of a trade; a second (meta) model looks at the primary's signal plus context and decides WHETHER to act and how much. Separates "which way" from "should I bet at all".
meta-labeling.coined: Marcos López de Prado, 2018 — "Advances in Financial Machine Learning" (Wiley), chapter 3.
meta-labeling.intuition: The tipster picks the horse; the risk manager decides whether this particular tip, from this tipster, in these conditions, deserves money. The meta model learns the primary's failure modes — sometimes its most valuable output is "skip". Our kb arms most-wrong caller being most profitable is exactly why sizing is a separate skill.
meta-labeling.math: Primary: side = sign(f(x)). Meta: P(win | side, features) = g(side, x'); bet iff expected value at the actual price clears a margin, size by (half-)Kelly on that P(win).
meta-labeling.here: pt6 is the meta-trader logit (7 features over the shared signal — docs/MODEL_INTERNALS.md §166): bet iff EV>0, half-Kelly size. sev0.html documents the live bug where p_win tracked the ask (+0.26 weight) so "EV>0" always fired — and the meta-labeling discipline that fixed it.
meta-labeling.code:
pw6 = pt6_logit.predict(features)          # P(win | side, context)
ev6 = pw6 * 100 - (askp + feep)            # bet only if ev6 >= margin

regime.what: A persistent market "mood" — calm vs violent, trending vs chopping, informed vs noisy — during which relationships hold, until the regime switches and yesterday's best model becomes today's worst.
regime.coined: The word is old; regime-switching as formal econometrics is James Hamilton, 1989 (Markov-switching model, Econometrica).
regime.intuition: A road can be dry or icy. The same steering that wins on dry pavement crashes on ice — the skill isn't one driving style, it's knowing which road you're on. Measured here: arm rankings inverted within 24 hours (kb4 +4.7% → −3.7%); band coverage collapsed from 0.827 (calm) to 0.518 (violent) under one-regime bands.
regime.math: Operationally: bucket windows by trailing σ (calm/normal/elevated/violent) or by trailing market accuracy. The M8 gate: stand down when the market's own recent accuracy over REGIME_LOOKBACK=20 windows drops below REGIME_FLOOR=0.62.
regime.here: REGIME_LOOKBACK/REGIME_FLOOR (M8) in btc_rl/online.py; σ-regime buckets condition the conformal bands; Fixed-Share exists because regimes rotate the best arm. Regime tables on experiment_review.html, ab_dashboard.html, metrics_lab.html, sev0.html.
regime.code:
REGIME_LOOKBACK = 20   # windows of market-accuracy signal
REGIME_FLOOR = 0.62    # stand down below this (M8), btc_rl/online.py

oracle-regret.what: The oracle is the impossible perfect player — it always knew the outcome or always picked the best arm. Regret is the gap between what you earned and what the oracle would have: the price of not knowing.
oracle-regret.coined: Regret in repeated decisions traces to James Hannan (1957) and became the central objective of online learning theory; "oracle" as the perfect-information benchmark is standard theory usage — exact coinage not verified here.
oracle-regret.intuition: After the race you can compute what betting perfectly would have paid. You'll never match it — but HOW FAR you fall short, per dollar, is the honest ceiling-to-floor measure of your decision quality, separate from whether the market was generous that day.
oracle-regret.math: regret = (oracle EV − achieved EV) per $1, cumulated or rolling. In expert-advice settings, algorithms like Fixed-Share carry provable bounds on regret vs the best (sequence of) experts.
oracle-regret.here: docs/MODEL_INTERNALS.md §6 computes the utopian counterfactual (oracle EV) and the desk's regret; metrics_lab.html shows the "Oracle regret / $1" headline stat; the M1 gate on sev0.html is "regret vs best fixed arm 2.7% → <1%/$1 over rolling 100 windows". (The site's brand "BTC 7PM Oracle" borrows the same word.)
oracle-regret.code:
regret = oracle_ev - desk_ev               # per $1, rolling windows
# metrics_lab.html renders mi.oracle.regret as the headline stat

monte-carlo.what: Answering a hard probability question by simulating it many times with random draws and counting the results, instead of solving formulas. Want the range of likely bankroll paths? Roll the dice 10,000 times in software.
monte-carlo.coined: Named by Nicholas Metropolis after the Monaco casino; developed by Stanislaw Ulam, John von Neumann and colleagues at Los Alamos in the late 1940s (Metropolis & Ulam, "The Monte Carlo Method", 1949).
monte-carlo.intuition: If you can't compute the odds of a card game, deal a million hands and count. Here: simulate the desk's future equity path many times at its measured win rate — the 5th-95th percentile of the simulated paths is a cone the real path should live inside. Escaping the cone = the model being wrong, in public.
monte-carlo.math: Draw N random paths from the estimated process (Bernoulli wins at p̂, real payout odds); statistic ≈ its distribution over paths. Error shrinks like 1/√N.
monte-carlo.here: home.html's equity chart draws 5th-95th Monte-Carlo cones behind each live line at the desk's measured win rate — the falsifiability layer.
monte-carlo.code:
// home.html: simulate paths at pHat, take 5th-95th percentiles
// live line escaping its cone => model wrong in public

persistence.what: The forecast that predicts no change: price in 15 minutes = price now. The humblest possible model — and in efficient markets, brutally hard to beat.
persistence.coined: Meteorology's classic no-skill benchmark ("tomorrow's weather = today's"); exact coinage not verified here. Its financial twin is the random-walk hypothesis: if prices already embed all information, no-change is near-optimal.
persistence.intuition: The bar every clever model must clear before earning respect. The crypto forecasting literature's recurring finding — models struggle to beat a random walk at short horizons — matches this project's own five-attempt "model axis is exhausted" negative result. MASE exists precisely to measure you against this floor.
persistence.math: ŷ_{t+h} = y_t. Its errors define the denominator of MASE/MSSE; "beating persistence" means MASE < 1 on the same slots.
persistence.here: btc_rl/agents.py class PersistenceAgent (Level 0: "tomorrow looks like today. The bar every RL agent must clear"); the naive errors in btc_rl/online.py's MASE computation. On every tier-1 page: index.html, live_training.html, live_online.html, metrics_lab.html.
persistence.src: Short-horizon crypto ML vs random walk: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405918821000027 (docs/RESEARCH_BASELINE.md, crypto section)

kalshi.what: A US-regulated (CFTC designated contract market) exchange for event contracts: binary yes/no bets on real-world outcomes, priced 1c-99c, settling at $1 if the event happens and $0 if not. This project trades its hourly "BTC above X at 7pm EDT?" markets on paper.
kalshi.coined: Founded 2018 by Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara; live since 2021. With Polymarket it passed ~$150B lifetime volume by April 2026, per the survey literature — an active academic testbed.
kalshi.intuition: A prediction market's price IS a probability: a YES trading at 62c means the crowd, weighted by money, thinks 62%. That's why the market itself is our benchmark forecaster (mkt_p_up) — beating it, not beating a coin, is the real game. Fees: 7% x P x (1−P) x 100 per contract, rounded up.
kalshi.math: P(event) ≈ price/100 under the Wolfers-Zitzewitz conditions for interpreting binary contract prices as mean trader beliefs. EV per contract = P·100 − (ask + fee).
kalshi.here: Market data via btc_rl/sources.py; fee model kalshi_fee_c in btc_rl/metrics.py; mkt_p_up as the reference forecaster throughout btc_rl/online.py. Every page: home.html, live_online.html, metrics_lab.html, ab_dashboard.html.
kalshi.src: Prices as probabilities: https://www.nber.org/papers/w12200 ; Kalshi calibration study: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19520 (docs/RESEARCH_BASELINE.md 2.4-2.5)

strike.what: The threshold price written into the contract. Our market asks: "will BTC be above the strike at 7pm EDT?" Everything the models predict is ultimately relative to this line.
strike.coined: Options-market terminology (the price at which a deal is "struck"); exact origin of the term not verified here.
strike.intuition: The strike turns a price forecast into a yes/no question. BTC at $110,000 with a $109,750 strike isn't "high or low" — it's "$250 of cushion, versus how much the price wiggles in the minutes left". That cushion-vs-wiggle ratio (distance/σ) is the single most informative feature in tier 2.
strike.math: P(yes) = P(price_T > strike). With a normal approximation: ≈ Φ((price_now − strike)/σ_remaining) — the z-score of the cushion.
strike.here: Parsed from Kalshi tickers in btc_rl/sources.py; strike-distance features in btc_rl/features.py; every kb arm and foundation-model arm converts forecasts to P(above strike) in btc_rl/online.py. On home.html, live_online.html, ab_dashboard.html, experiment_review.html.
strike.code:
dist_sigma = (price_now - strike) / sigma_remaining
# the cushion-vs-wiggle feature, btc_rl/features.py

bid-ask.what: The two prices on every order book: the bid is the highest price anyone will pay right now; the ask is the lowest price anyone will sell for. The gap (spread) is the cost of trading immediately.
bid-ask.coined: Open-outcry market vocabulary, centuries old; exact origin not verified here.
bid-ask.intuition: At any moment there are two prices, not one: what you'd get selling instantly (bid) and what you'd pay buying instantly (ask). Cross the gap twice and you've paid the spread for nothing — on a 2c spread at 60c that's a big chunk of a small edge. The mid ((bid+ask)/2) is the fair-value estimate.
bid-ask.math: spread = ask − bid; mid = (bid + ask)/2. Our EV math always charges the real ask plus fee: cost_c = ask_c + fee_c; break-even P = cost_c/100.
bid-ask.here: Top-of-book bid/ask from btc_rl/sources.py; ask_c is the price in bet_ev (btc_rl/treatments.py) and every trader's cost model in btc_rl/online.py; book imbalance uses both sizes. On live_online.html, home.html, metrics_lab.html, ab_dashboard.html.
bid-ask.code:
cost = ask_c + fee                          # treatments.py bet_ev
return (100.0 - cost) / cost if won else -1.0

sharpe.what: Return per unit of risk: average excess return divided by the standard deviation of returns. The classic "was the reward worth the ride?" number.
sharpe.coined: William F. Sharpe, 1966 ("Mutual Fund Performance") — he called it the reward-to-variability ratio; the field named it after him. Sharpe shared the 1990 Nobel in economics.
sharpe.intuition: +20% by a smooth climb and +20% by a rollercoaster are different achievements. Dividing by the wobble rewards the smooth path. But it needs many periods to estimate: on ~4 days of live desk data a Sharpe is noise, which is why this project reports net÷drawdown instead and worries about selection bias (deflated Sharpe) first.
sharpe.math: SR = (mean(r) − r_f)/std(r), usually annualized by √(periods/year). The deflated Sharpe ratio (Bailey & López de Prado) corrects it for how many strategies you tried before picking this one.
sharpe.here: Deliberately NOT reported (metrics_lab.html and docs/RESEARCH_BASELINE.md 3.5 explain why: too little live data; DSR machinery matters more). The scoreboard ranks by net ÷ max drawdown instead (scripts/standings.py).
sharpe.code:
# not computed here by design — 4 days of data makes SR noise;
# ranking uses net / max_drawdown (scripts/run_audit.py)

welford.what: A one-pass, numerically stable way to keep a running mean and variance as data streams in — no storing of history, no catastrophic cancellation.
welford.coined: B. P. Welford, 1962 (Technometrics). The textbook two-pass variance formula fails on streams; Welford's update is the standard fix.
welford.intuition: You want "average and spread so far" updated on every new number without re-reading old ones. Welford keeps three counters (n, mean, M2) and updates them with two subtractions and a multiply — the spread estimate is always ready and never blows up.
welford.math: n += 1; δ = x − mean; mean += δ/n; M2 += δ·(x − mean); variance = M2/(n−1). Note δ uses the OLD mean and the second factor the NEW one — that asymmetry is the trick.
welford.here: The SPRT's online variance in btc_rl/treatments.py (self.m2) — the plug-in normal LLR divides by this variance, which is why the variance floor exists (a near-zero Welford variance once produced LLR 123, a false promotion on numerical noise).
welford.code:
delta = d - self.mean                      # treatments.py SPRT.add
self.mean += delta / self.n
self.m2 += delta * (d - self.mean)

epsilon-greedy.what: The simplest exploration rule: with probability ε do something random, otherwise do the best-known thing. ε usually decays over time as knowledge accumulates.
epsilon-greedy.coined: Standard reinforcement-learning practice, canonical in Watkins' Q-learning work (1989) and the Sutton & Barto textbook; exact coinage not verified here.
epsilon-greedy.intuition: Order your favorite dish 95% of the time; roll a die for the other 5% so you never stop discovering. Crude compared to LinUCB's targeted optimism — random exploration wastes tries on known-bad arms — but nearly unbeatable for simplicity and robustness.
epsilon-greedy.math: a = random arm with prob ε, else argmax_a Q(s,a). Here ε decays linearly across training epochs from EPSILON_START toward a floor.
epsilon-greedy.here: btc_rl/agents.py: TabularQAgent and LinearQAgent explore ε-greedy while training (EPSILON_START and decay in btc_rl/config.py, decay_epsilon in agents.py). The ε schedule is visible on live_training.html.
epsilon-greedy.code:
if explore and self.rng.random() < self.epsilon:   # agents.py
    return self.rng.randrange(len(config.ACTION_DELTAS))

pesaran-timmermann.what: A significance test for directional accuracy: is your up/down hit rate better than what your own guessing habits and the market's base rates would produce by luck?
pesaran-timmermann.coined: M. Hashem Pesaran & Allan Timmermann, 1992 — "A Simple Nonparametric Test of Predictive Performance" (Journal of Business & Economic Statistics).
pesaran-timmermann.intuition: If the market goes up 60% of the time and you predict "up" 60% of the time, you'll be right about 52% by pure luck — 52% is not skill, it's arithmetic. The PT test computes that no-skill baseline from the marginal frequencies and asks how many standard deviations above it you really are.
pesaran-timmermann.math: z = (p̂ − p*)/sqrt(V̂ − V*), where p̂ is your hit rate and p* = p_pred·p_actual + (1−p_pred)(1−p_actual) is the luck rate implied by the marginals. |z| > 1.96 = significant at 5%.
pesaran-timmermann.here: btc_rl/metrics.py pt_test() (needs ≥ 20 settled predictions); scored per tier-1 arm — the honest version of the 47-53% direction finding. On experiment_review.html.
pesaran-timmermann.code:
p_star = py*pa + (1-py)*(1-pa)             # metrics.py pt_test
return (p_hat - p_star) / math.sqrt(v_hat - v_star)

mde.what: The smallest true effect your experiment, at its current sample size, would reliably detect at your chosen significance and power. Anything smaller is invisible to the test — not absent, just invisible.
mde.coined: From the sample-size / experiment-design literature that grew out of the Neyman-Pearson framework and Cohen's power-analysis work; the "MDE" name itself was popularized by the online A/B-testing industry (the Kohavi lineage of experimentation platforms) — exact first use not verified here.
mde.intuition: A telescope has a resolution: stars closer together than that limit look like one star, no matter how real the gap is. MDE is the resolution of your experiment. If your MDE is 12¢ and the effect you care about is 2¢, the test cannot see what you're looking for — running it to the end and reading "not significant" would tell you nothing.
mde.math: For a one-sided test on a mean with standard error SE: MDE ≈ (z_{1−α} + z_{1−β})·SE. Tighter α (multiple-testing corrections) and higher required power both push the MDE up; only more data (shrinking SE like 1/√n) pulls it down.
mde.here: Computed per challenger in scripts/emit_decision_board.py and shown on the Metrics Lab Decision board (tooltip on the Power@2¢ column, and in each card's evidence line on board.html). At n=168 the M8 regime gate's MDE is ~12¢/$1 against a pre-registered 2¢ edge — a fixed-horizon test at family-wise α simply cannot resolve the effect yet, which is why the desk decides with a sequential SPRT instead.
mde.code:
mde = (z_alpha + z_beta) * se     # scripts/emit_decision_board.py
# family-wise one-sided alpha, beta from config

power.what: The probability your test detects an effect of a given size when that effect is really there: power = 1 − β, where β is the miss rate. Low power means a "not significant" result is mostly a statement about your sample size, not about the world.
power.coined: Jerzy Neyman & Egon Pearson, 1933 ("On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses", Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society) — the paper that split testing errors into type I (false alarm, α) and type II (miss, β) and made power a first-class design quantity.
power.intuition: A smoke detector's sensitivity. α is how often it screams at burnt toast; power is how often it actually goes off in a real fire. A detector that almost never false-alarms but sleeps through 98% of fires is not cautious, it's useless — and that is precisely a low-powered experiment reading "no significant difference".
power.math: For a one-sided test of mean effect δ with standard error SE: power = Φ(δ/SE − z_{1−α}). Power rises with the true effect size, with n (through SE), and with a looser α; multiple-testing corrections that shrink α also drain power.
power.here: The Power@2¢ column of the Decision board (metrics_lab.html, from results/decision_board.json): the chance of detecting the pre-registered 2¢/$1 edge at the current n under the family-wise α. At n=168 it is ~2% — a fixed-horizon test would be theater at this sample size, which is exactly why promotion decisions run through the sequential SPRT (evidence accumulates, no fixed n) instead.
power.code:
power = 1 - norm.cdf(z_alpha - edge / se)   # emit_decision_board.py
# power_at_edge in decision_board.json, per challenger

bootstrap-ci.what: A confidence interval built by resampling your own data with replacement thousands of times and reading the spread of the recomputed statistic — no normality assumption, no formula for the standard error required.
bootstrap-ci.coined: Bradley Efron, 1979 ("Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife", Annals of Statistics). The name is the old "pull yourself up by your bootstraps" joke made rigorous: the sample stands in for the population it came from.
bootstrap-ci.intuition: You can't rerun history, but you can shuffle it: draw 168 windows from your own 168 with replacement, recompute the mean Δ, repeat 2000 times. The scatter of those 2000 means is an honest picture of how much your estimate wobbles — including the fat tails and jackpot windows a normal approximation smooths over, which is why it sits next to the normal CI here rather than being replaced by it.
bootstrap-ci.math: Resample n rows with replacement B times; compute the statistic on each resample; the percentile interval is the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the B values. P(Δ>0) is just the fraction of resamples with a positive mean. Here B = boot_n = 2000, seeded (boot_seed) so every page load reproduces the same interval.
bootstrap-ci.here: The 95% CI and P(Δ>0) columns of the Decision board are the bootstrap versions (boot_ci95, p_gt0_boot, p_gt_edge_boot in results/decision_board.json, computed by scripts/emit_decision_board.py); board.html cards show the same interval. The M8 regime gate's [−0.0¢, +12.0¢] straddling zero — while P(Δ>0) reads ~97% — is the bootstrap being honest about a lumpy, right-skewed effect.
bootstrap-ci.code:
idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=(boot_n, n))  # seeded, emit_decision_board.py
boots = diffs[idx].mean(axis=1)
lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5]); p_gt0 = (boots > 0).mean()
